verses.translation_literal: Praise Yah! Sing to YHWH a song new, his praise in the assembly of the faithful ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hallelujah! Lift your voices to the LORD, and let the song be one no one has sung before. Let his praise rise in the gathering of those who have held fast to him.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the opening cry of the psalm's last-but-one movement, and it is a command to a crowd, not a private prayer: both verbs are plural imperatives. Play it as a call across a gathering, to people already standing together.

The KJV's 'saints' softens nothing but shifts the register: it sounds like a class of holy persons set apart. The Hebrew ḥăsîdîm are people marked by ḥesed, covenant loyalty, so the 'assembly' is the community of those who keep faith with YHWH. 'New song' is a stock summons in the Psalter (Ps 33:3, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9), calling for fresh praise to meet a fresh act of God. Radak reads it as a call to compose a song beyond the written ones. Note the word 'praise' returns as a noun, tĕhillātô: the verb and the noun stay in the same root as 'Hallelujah'.

philological_notes.note: Those who practice or are shown covenant loyalty (ḥesed). 'Saints' in the KJV is a later theological label; here it names the covenant community.
'A new song', a fixed phrase for praise answering a fresh act of God. Radak takes it as the people composing a song of their own beyond the written ones.

verses.translation_literal: Let Israel rejoice in his makers; sons of Zion, let them exult in their king.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let Israel be glad in the One who made him. Let the children of Zion burst into joy over their King.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two parallel lines, two names for the same community: Israel and the 'sons of Zion', a phrase that places the singers in Jerusalem, where the king is enthroned. Play the second line a step louder than the first.

The odd form is 'ōśāyw, 'his makers', plural in Hebrew while the sense is singular. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri all call it a plural of majesty, as in Isaiah 54:5 and Job 35:10. The KJV's 'him that made him' quietly irons this out into a singular, which is right in meaning but hides the strangeness of the grammar. Malbim also notes a nice difference between the two verbs: śāmaḥ is rejoicing in general; gîl is joy at something new, so the sons of Zion keep finding fresh joy in their king. 'King' here is YHWH, and the verse prepares the royal imagery that the sword and chains of the later verses assume.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'in his makers'. A plural form with singular meaning, read as a plural of majesty by the medieval commentators.
To exult. Malbim distinguishes gîl, joy over something new, from śimḥâ, joy in general.

verses.translation_literal: Let them praise his name with dancing; with tambourine and lyre let them make music to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them praise his name in the dance, feet answering the beat. Let the tambourine strike and the lyre ring out, and let them make music for him.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the praise gets a body. This is the dance-and-drum celebration that ancient Israelite women led after victory (Exod 15:20; the picture Malbim recalls) and that greeted returning warriors. Stage it as movement, not as a hymn sung in rows.

The KJV's 'in the dance' is fine, though 'dance' in a church setting often suggests something more sedate; māḥôl is a circle or line dance. The tōp is the hand-frame drum, 'timbrel' in the KJV, an archaic word English readers no longer picture; kinnôr is a lyre, not a 'harp', and is the instrument of David. The verse also repeats the praise-verbs: hillēl and zimmēr, to praise and to make music, so the Hebrew sings in two stacked registers: name and instruments.

philological_notes.note: Dancing, especially round or circle dancing, often with timbrels. Malbim links it to the women's dance after the Exodus.
A hand-held frame drum, the 'timbrel' of the KJV.
A lyre, not a 'harp' in the modern sense.

verses.translation_literal: For YHWH is taking pleasure in his people; he adorns the humble ones with salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD delights in his people. He dresses the lowly in victory, and wears it as beauty on them.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reason for the party: a verse of pure motive. The verb rōṣeh is a participle, so the pleasure is ongoing: YHWH is delighted right now, not once. Give the line warmth, not fanfare.

The KJV's 'will beautify' turns a present or habitual verb into a future promise; the Hebrew yĕpā'ēr is an imperfect that can be either, and the context of present praise reads naturally as present. 'Beautify' is also good: the root pā'ar is about adorning, as one decks a bride or a priest with splendour. BBE's 'crown of salvation' guesses at the image. 'The humble' ('ănāwîm) are the poor and lowly, those with no power of their own, which is why salvation is something put on them as a gift. The surprise to hear is who gets the honour: not the strong but the lowly.

philological_notes.note: To adorn or glorify, from the same root as 'splendour' (pĕ'ēr). Salvation becomes the adornment of the humble.
The humble or lowly. Radak says Israel is chosen because it is the humblest of nations; Malbim takes the 'ănāwîm to be the righteous within the people.

verses.translation_literal: Let the faithful ones exult in honor; let them sing for joy upon their beds.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the faithful exult in the honor he has given them. Let them sing for joy even there, upon their beds.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns inward. After public dancing, the song follows the singers home, to the place of privacy and night. The surprise is the beds: joy is not left in the temple courtyard.

The KJV's 'saints be joyful in glory' flattens two distinct things. 'Ya'lĕzû' is a strong verb, to exult or triumph, and kābôd is weighty honor or glory, the reputation the faithful receive from God. 'Upon their beds' is literal, and the old interpreters differ widely on its meaning: Ibn Ezra reads solitary singing in the night; Metzudat David, rest in their own land; Meiri and Malbim, a hint of rest after death. Keep it open. As an actor, play the line quiet and close, the voice dropping, to mark the change from the crowd to the private room.

philological_notes.note: 'Upon their beds'. Read as night-time solitude (Ibn Ezra), repose in their land (Metzudat David), or rest after death (Meiri, Malbim).
To exult, a stronger word than ordinary gladness.

verses.translation_literal: Exaltations of God [be] in their throat, and a sword of mouths in their hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the praise of God rise high in their throats, rolling out loud and deep. And in the same hands that were raised in worship, let a blade be held, sharp on both its edges.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two things are held at once, one in the throat and one in the hand, and the verse sets them side by side with no verb between them. The singers do not put the sword down to sing, or the song down to fight. Play both lines as one action.

The KJV's "mouth" softens the Hebrew gārôn, which is the throat, the place the voice comes from. Meiri, in the packet, reads it as a loud voice and cites Isaiah 58:1, "cry aloud from the throat", so this is full-voiced praise and not a murmur. The KJV's "twoedged" is accurate in sense but hides the Hebrew image: the sword is literally "a sword of mouths" (pîpiyyôt, a doubled form of peh, "mouth"). Metzudat Zion explains that the edge of a blade is called a "mouth", as in Judges 3, where Ehud's sword had two. So the audience hears a sword with two mouths, and hears it right after the praise sung by a throat. The pairing of mouths with a throat is my own observation of the wording, not something the commentaries say. Radak and Meiri each read the sword as cutting from both sides.

philological_notes.note: Plural of pîpiyyâ, a doubled form built on peh, "mouth". It names the edges of a blade, so a "two-edged" sword is literally one with two mouths. Metzudat Zion compares Judges 3, where Ehud's sword is said to have "two mouths" (shtê pêyôt).
"In their throat", the organ of voice, not the mouth as the KJV has it. Meiri takes it as a loud voice and compares Isaiah 58:1.

verses.translation_literal: to do vengeance on the nations, rebukes among the peoples,
verses.translation_dramatic: to carry out vengeance upon the nations, and bring rebuke down among the peoples.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hard verse, and the actors must not soften it. Keep the infinitive that continues from the sword: the sword is for this, vengeance. The delivery is cold and formal, as if reading a sentence.

The KJV's 'heathen' is an old word for non-Israelites and carries a contempt the Hebrew gôyim does not: it means simply 'nations'. 'Punishments' for tôkēḥôt is a fair rendering, but the word is also 'rebukes' or 'reproofs': the same root is used for arguing a case (Radak reads it as the nations arguing with their kings, asking why this has come on them). The shift from nĕqāmâ, vengeance as justice restored, to tôkēḥôt, discipline, marks that the aim is judgment, not random slaughter. The medieval interpreters mostly place the scene at the end of days, when God's justice puts the nations right (Ibn Ezra, Meiri).

philological_notes.note: Vengeance in the sense of just recompense, usually carried out by God or a legitimate authority on his behalf.
Reproofs, corrections, punishments. Metzudat Zion takes it as a judgment of sufferings, as in Job 33:19.

verses.translation_literal: To bind their kings with fetters, and their honored ones with shackles of iron.
verses.translation_dramatic: To bind their kings in fetters. To bind the great ones among them, the honored and the proud, in shackles of iron. Let the men who wore honor like a crown learn what it is to wear a chain.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the end of the sentence that began in verse 6, and it moves up the ladder of rank: kings first, then the honored ones beneath them. These are the people whom their own societies respect, and the verse says they will be bound like anyone else.

The KJV has "chains" and "fetters of iron", which blur two different Hebrew words. Zikkîm is a kind of fetter or chain, and Metzudat Zion cites Jeremiah 40:1, where Jeremiah is bound in zikkîm. Kavlê barzel is a second word for restraints, glossed there as chain-like. The KJV's "nobles" for nikhbedêhem also loses the sound of the Hebrew: it is literally "their honored ones", the same root as kābôd, "honor, glory", set against kavlê, "shackles". The two words differ by one consonant, so the ear hears the honored ones and the shackles almost as one sound. This sound play is my own reading, not one the commentaries make. Ibn Ezra reads the verse as the natural next step after vengeance on the nations, and the kings are named because they too are bound.

The verse shows iron as the strongest restraint available: the honored ones get the heaviest hold, and the text leaves out any pity for them. Act the line with the weight of an official sentence being carried out, not with rage.

philological_notes.note: A kind of fetter or chain. Rashi glosses it with a word for chains, and Metzudat Zion cites Jeremiah 40:1, "he was bound in zikkîm". The KJV renders it "chains".

A passive participle, "the honored ones", with a possessive: "their honored ones". Metzudat David glosses it as the honored among them. It shares a root with kābôd, "honor, glory", where the KJV's "nobles" names only rank.

verses.translation_literal: to do among them judgment written; it is splendor for all his faithful ones. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: to carry out on them the judgment that is written. This is splendor for all his faithful ones. Hallelujah!
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm closes with a verdict and a cheer. Read 'judgment written' slowly, as a sentence already on the page, then lift into the last two words as a shout. The frame closes: Hallelujah opened the psalm and now ends it.

The KJV's 'this honour have all his saints' reads the Hebrew as if the saints possess the honor; the Hebrew simply says 'splendor it is for all his faithful ones', with hādār, majesty or splendor, as a predicate, so the judgment itself is the splendor. Which writing is meant is left open. Rashi cites Ezekiel 25:14 on Edom and says David prophesied the end; Metzudat David adds that the judgment was not yet written in David's time but will be. Malbim hears the Canaanite laws in the Torah. Notice also the problem a modern reader feels: the psalm calls this honor. Directors should not apologize for it, but should let the audience feel that the text claims the sentence is God's, not the singers'.

philological_notes.note: 'Judgment written'. Rashi points to Ezekiel 25:14; Metzudat David says it was not yet written in David's day but will be at the redemption.
Splendor, majesty, honor. Metzudat Zion glosses it as beauty.
